title: Mystery deaths in Koodathil mansion: Court clerk kept Kerala cops on toes till a forensic journal flipped the script
content: A cop-turned-court clerk, Ravindran Nair, had Kerala police run in circles for almost a decade before he was arrested on Tuesday for the alleged murder of Jayamadhavan Nair, the last legal heir of Koodathil family at Karamana in Thiruvananthapuram. The family, which owned vast swathes of land at prime locations in Thiruvananthapuram, was battered by a series of deaths between 1991 and 2017. All the deaths were passed off as 'natural' by cops until Jayamadhavan was allegedly murdered on April 1, 2017. No brainer turns hard puzzle For the police, it seemed like a slam dunk case. The autopsy report showed blood stains on the left side of the body. There was a contusion on the left side of forehead and abrasions on nose and right forearm. Ravindran Nair's statements on timing of the incident, mode of death and transportation to hospital, crumbled as contradictions kept popping up. Little did police realise that his three decades of experience in handling murder case files in court and his brief stint as a policeman earlier in his career had honed his counter-narrative skills. During hours of interrogation, Ravindran Nair didn't bat an eyelid. "His expression said it all. It was like, I am not going to confess, if you have it in you, you can prove the crime. We knew he was lying about everything, but without a confession, we couldn't move ahead," recalled retired Crime Branch ACP M K Zulfikar, who had probed the case. "He had told us that the day after Jayamadhavan's death, he had dropped off his daughter at a tutorial. When we checked with the principal, he said it was a holiday. Ravindran still stuck with his statement," said Zulfikar. Any report filed in the court would be met with a counter affidavit busting the case painstakingly built by the police. His rich network of contacts gave him easy access to police reports in the court and he was always ready with responses. The Crime Branch report filed in the High Court noted that it was clear that the investigation team has been blocked using several delaying tactics by Ravindran who filed trivial suits time and again. He was well-versed in law and has garnered experience as a court staff for several years, the report said. When the Crime Branch took over the case in 2019, Ravindran Nair also faced a parallel case of cheating. A family member had filed a complaint against him saying that he had bequeathed 33 cents of land from Jayamadhavan using a forged will. This sparked further suspicion that all the previous deaths in the family may have been executed as part of an organised murder plot. "We could prove that the will was not executed in the presence of Jayamadhavan. One of the witnesses to the will was Leela, the housemaid, who didn't even know how to read and write," Zulfikar said. When the police got an order from the court for a forensic examination of the will, Ravindran filed an objection in the High Court saying that it be examined at the Central lab instead of state lab only to delay the process further. The court then ordered examination of the will at the FSL, Thiruvananthapuram, and it was proved that the will was forged. Technology comes to help The legal battles wouldn't stop. Eventually, a casual reference of an international forensic journal by an investigator opened up possibilities of forensic biomechanics which proved that death of Jayamadhavan was a homicide. Forensic biomechanics uses principles of mechanical engineering, biology and forensic science to understand nature, pattern and severity of injuries. "It hadn't been used in Kerala before. We got to know it from an article on Medwin publishers and thought of using it in this case. It is generally used by foreign agencies in accident investigations," said Viju N, former ACP, City Crime Branch, who now serves at the Intelligence HQ. The police approached the Department of Bioscience and Engineering at NIT, Calicut. "We had to prove if Jayamadhavan had a free fall or a forced fall...
